title: Killing Coding Agent Slop With Adversarial Self-Play
summary: Vendor post arguing that pairing a generator agent with an adversarial verifier agent in a loop reduces slop, citing small self-run SlopCodeBench results.

assertions.quote: human review doesn't scale to LLM volumes. At this point, my coding agents produce code much faster than I can review it.

verdicts.note: The SmartBear/Cisco review study found defect detection drops beyond ~200-400 LOC per session; AI makes large PRs cheap to produce.

assertions.quote: deterministic checks can't catch every subjective dimension, including design, quality standards, and complexity.

verdicts.note: Linters and agent rules catch local smells, but architecture and coupling decisions still lack automated checks. Tooling is improving.

assertions.quote: the harness takes a goal specification as input and runs two coding agents in a loop: one generates code; the other reviews and tests it.

verdicts.note: Separate verifier/critic setups improve outputs in several studies and vendor reports, but the evidence here is a small self-run benchmark subset with two trials and large token costs.

assertions.quote: A single agent with shared context doesn't do as good a job as an independent verifier.

verdicts.note: Fresh-context reviewers avoid self-confirmation and context bloat; plausible and commonly practiced but little hard evidence.

assertions.quote: Generation is a fundamentally hard and unforgiving search problem. Verification is simpler.

verdicts.note: Verification cost largely determines whether AI help saves time; field studies find gains concentrate where outputs are cheap to check.

assertions.quote: By checkpoint three, the one-shot agent on file_backup passed only 16% of the earlier checkpoints' tests

verdicts.note: Consistent with long-horizon benchmarks such as SlopCodeBench and with studies of AI-code churn and duplication. Evidence is early but points the same way.

assertions.quote: Smarter models reward hack more, especially over long horizons.

verdicts.note: Reward hacking on tests (special-casing, weakening or deleting tests) is documented by labs and in agent evaluations, though frequency varies by model and setup.

assertions.quote: This abstraction lets us treat the spec as a durable artifact and code as the disposable implementation, much like a traditional compiler.

verdicts.note: Specs help align agents, but code is still what runs; specs drift from implementation unless continuously maintained, and practitioners like Pocock report specs-only workflows failing.
